title: Back in my old bedroom
instructions: Read the article about young adults who move back in with their parents. Complete the sentences (1–9) by choosing the correct ending (A–L). There are two extra endings that you do not need to use. There is an example (0) at the beginning.
instructionsHu: Olvasd el a cikket a szüleikhez visszaköltöző fiatal felnőttekről. Fejezd be a mondatokat (1–9) a megfelelő mondatvég (A–L) kiválasztásával. Két mondatvég felesleges. A 0. a példa.

passage.title: Back in my old bedroom
passage.subtitle: More young adults than ever are moving back in with their parents after university. One of them describes what it is really like.

blocks.text: The posters are still on the wall. When I moved back into my childhood bedroom last September, aged twenty-three, with a degree in biology and no job, the first thing I noticed was that nothing had changed: the same purple curtains, the same glow-in-the-dark stars on the ceiling, the same school photos my mum refused to take down. The second thing I noticed was how small the bed was.

I am far from alone. In Britain, around a quarter of people aged 20 to 34 now live with their parents, and the figure is even higher in southern Europe. Sociologists have a name for us – the 'boomerang generation' – because we leave home and then come straight back. The reasons are mostly practical. Rents have risen much faster than starting salaries, and many graduates, like me, spend months looking for a job in their field. Moving home is, for many, the only way to save for a deposit on a flat.

What nobody tells you is how strange it feels emotionally. At university I had cooked my own meals, paid my own bills and decided for myself when to come home at night. Within a week of returning, I found myself behaving like a fifteen-year-old again: sulking when my dad asked where I was going, leaving my dishes in the sink, waiting for someone else to buy toilet paper. 'It's extremely common,' says family therapist Dr Rosa Lindqvist. 'When adult children move back, everyone tends to slip back into their old roles, because the house itself reminds them of who they used to be.'

Dr Lindqvist's advice to families is to have an honest conversation at the start, before problems build up. Who pays for what? Should the returning child contribute to the household costs, and if so, how much? Who does the cooking and cleaning? And – the question that, she says, causes more arguments than any other – does anyone need to be told when someone will be home late? 'Parents often expect the rules of the past to apply automatically,' she explains. 'The young person expects to be treated like a lodger. Both end up disappointed.'

In our house, that conversation came about a month too late, after a row about a pile of laundry that I still don't think was entirely my fault. We agreed that I would pay a small amount each month – far less than a real rent – and cook dinner twice a week. My parents agreed to stop asking about my job applications unless I mentioned them first. It sounds like a minor thing, but it made an enormous difference. I hadn't realised how much those well-meant questions had been adding to my stress.

There have been unexpected benefits, too. I've got to know my parents as people rather than just as Mum and Dad. My father, it turns out, has been secretly writing a detective novel for ten years, and my mother and I now go to an evening pottery class together. Dr Lindqvist says this is typical of families that handle the situation well: the relationship gradually changes from one between a parent and a child into something closer to a friendship between adults.

I start a new job in a laboratory in March, and by the summer I hope to have saved enough to move out again – this time, I hope, for good. I'll admit I'm looking forward to having my own kitchen. But I suspect that one day I'll look back on this year as a gift: a chance to see my parents differently, which most people never get.

example.prompt: When she moved back home, the writer found that her old bedroom
example.explanation: B – had been left exactly as it was before. Az első, ami feltűnt neki, hogy semmi sem változott a szobájában (ugyanazok a függönyök, csillagok, fényképek).
example.evidence: the first thing I noticed was that nothing had changed

items.prompt: Young adults like the writer are called the 'boomerang generation' because they
items.explanation: D – move out only to return soon afterwards. A bumeráng visszatér oda, ahonnan elhajították: a fiatalok elköltöznek otthonról, aztán hamar visszajönnek („leave home and then come straight back”).
items.evidence: because we leave home and then come straight back

wrongOptions.H: Az anyagi ok a visszaköltözés magyarázata, nem a „bumeráng” elnevezésé – a név magát a mozgást (elmenni, majd visszatérni) írja le.

items.prompt: Many graduates move back in with their parents because they
items.explanation: H – cannot otherwise afford to save for a place of their own. Sokaknak a hazaköltözés az egyetlen módja, hogy összegyűjtsék egy lakás önrészét („the only way to save for a deposit on a flat”).
items.evidence: Moving home is, for many, the only way to save for a deposit on a flat.

wrongOptions.D: Ez az elnevezést magyarázza (elmennek, majd visszajönnek), nem azt, hogy miért költöznek vissza.

items.prompt: Within a week of returning, the writer
items.explanation: F – began acting as if she were years younger. Egy héten belül úgy viselkedett, mint egy tizenöt éves: duzzogott, a mosogatóban hagyta a tányérjait, és várta, hogy más vegyen vécépapírt.
items.evidence: I found myself behaving like a fifteen-year-old again

wrongOptions.L: A szülei új oldalainak felfedezése később történt, és a hazatérés pozitív hozadéka – az első hét épp a régi szerepekbe való visszaesésről szólt.

items.prompt: According to Dr Lindqvist, family members slip back into old roles because the house
items.explanation: J – makes them remember who they were in the past. A terapeuta szerint maga a ház emlékezteti őket arra, kik voltak régen („reminds them of who they used to be”).
items.evidence: because the house itself reminds them of who they used to be

wrongOptions.B: Az, hogy a szoba változatlan maradt, az író saját élménye; a „had been left exactly as it was before” nyelvtanilag sem illik a „the house” után következő magyarázathoz.

items.explanation: A – discuss practical arrangements before tensions arise. Azt tanácsolja, hogy már az elején, a problémák kialakulása előtt beszéljék meg őszintén, ki miért fizet, ki főz és takarít.
items.evidence: Dr Lindqvist's advice to families is to have an honest conversation at the start, before problems build up.

wrongOptions.I: A teljes piaci lakbért senki sem javasolja; az írónál végül épp „far less than a real rent” összegben egyeztek meg.

items.prompt: The writer's parents agreed that they would
items.explanation: K – not raise the subject of her job search unless she did so first. A szülők megígérték, hogy nem kérdezgetik az álláspályázatairól, hacsak ő maga nem hozza szóba.
items.evidence: My parents agreed to stop asking about my job applications unless I mentioned them first.

wrongOptions.I: Nyelvtanilag illik, de tartalmilag hamis: csak egy kis havi összeget fizet, „far less than a real rent”.

items.prompt: Looking back, the writer realises that her parents' questions
items.explanation: E – had been making her more anxious than she knew. Csak utólag jött rá, mennyire növelték a stresszét a jó szándékú kérdések („I hadn't realised how much…”).
items.evidence: I hadn't realised how much those well-meant questions had been adding to my stress.

wrongOptions.B: A „had been left exactly as it was before” a szobára vonatkozik (példa), a kérdésekre értelmetlen.

items.explanation: L – discover sides of her parents she had never seen before. Megismerte a szüleit emberként: kiderült, hogy az apja tíz éve titokban krimit ír, az anyjával pedig együtt járnak fazekastanfolyamra.
items.evidence: My father, it turns out, has been secretly writing a detective novel for ten years

wrongOptions.G: A „see this year as a valuable opportunity” azt írja le, hogyan fog egyszer visszatekinteni erre az évre (9. mondat), nem azt, amit az otthonlakás most lehetővé tett.

items.prompt: The writer expects that one day she will
items.explanation: G – see this year as a valuable opportunity. Úgy gondolja, egyszer ajándékként tekint majd vissza erre az évre („look back on this year as a gift”), mert kevesen kapnak ilyen esélyt.
items.evidence: I suspect that one day I'll look back on this year as a gift
